hints: Think about what happens when the same solute is shaken with two immiscible liquids and allowed to settle into equilibrium.
walkthrough:
Picture the equilibrium system**
Imagine you shake a solute with water and $\text{CS}_2$ which do not mix. After shaking, the solute spreads itself between the two layers until equilibrium is reached. $K_{pc}$ simply compares how much is in one solvent compared to the other as concentrations.
Final answer: The ratio of the concentrations of a solute dissolved in two immiscible solvents at equilibrium.

hints: Start by finding the total mass of X actually shaken, using the 40.0 cm3 portion taken from the 100.0 cm3 flask containing 1.85 g.
Let y be the mass in the CS2 layer, then express both concentrations as mass divided by volume and set their ratio equal to 10.5.
walkthrough:
Find how much X you start with**
You do not shake all $1.85\text{ g}$. It was made up to $100.0\text{ cm}^3$ but only $40.0\text{ cm}^3$ is used. So mass taken = $$1.85 \times \frac{40.0}{100.0} = 0.74\text{ g}$$ Keep this number, it is your total mass balance.

Set up the partition expression**
Let $y$ = mass of $\text{X}$ in $\text{CS}_2$ layer in g. Then mass left in water = $0.74 - y$. Concentration is proportional to mass/volume, so: $$K_{pc} = \frac{y/25.0}{(0.74-y)/40.0} = 10.5$$ Solve: $40.0y = 10.5 \times 25.0 \times (0.74-y)$, giving $y = 0.642\text{ g}$ extracted into $\text{CS}_2$.

hints: Recall the link: double bonded C with 3 sigma regions is sp2, single bonded tetrahedral C with 4 sigma regions is sp3.
Count C=C carbons versus C-C single only carbons in each drawing, remembering each vertex is a CH group.
walkthrough:
Use double bonds as your counter**
Any carbon in a $\text{C=C}$ double bond has three electron domains and is $\text{sp}^2$ hybridised. Any carbon joined only by single $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ bonds has four domains and is $\text{sp}^3$ hybridised. There are no triple bonds, so $\text{sp} = 0$ everywhere.

Apply to the three structures**
Kekule has a 6-membered ring with 3 $\text{C=C}$, so all 6 C are $\text{sp}^2$. Dewar has 2 $\text{C=C}$ (4 C are $\text{sp}^2$) plus 2 bridgehead C joined only by singles (2 C are $\text{sp}^3$). Ladenburg prismane has no double bonds at all, all faces are single bonds, so all 6 C are $\text{sp}^3$.

Final answer: Kekule benzene: 0 sp, 6 sp2, 0 sp3
Dewar benzene: 0 sp, 4 sp2, 2 sp3
Ladenburg benzene (prismane): 0 sp, 0 sp2, 6 sp3

hints: Recall the geometry around each sp2 carbon in benzene and the overall flat shape this creates.
Think about which bonds contain pi electron density in the delocalised ring versus the C-H bonds.
walkthrough:
Build the shape from the carbon geometry**
Each carbon in delocalised benzene is $\text{sp}^2$ with three $\sigma$ bonds in a plane at $120^{\circ}$. Joined in a ring, this gives a perfectly flat regular hexagon with all carbons and hydrogens coplanar.

Sort sigma versus pi**
The framework between carbons is $\sigma$ bonds, with one $p$ orbital left on each carbon overlapping sideways to give a delocalised $\pi$ system above and below the ring. So $\text{C-C}$ has $\sigma + \pi$ character, while each $\text{C-H}$ is a simple localised $\sigma$ bond only.

Final answer: Planar hexagon, each C trigonal planar with C-C-H / C-C-C angle $120^{\circ}$.
C-C bonds contain sigma plus delocalised pi system, C-H bonds are sigma only.

hints: Compare the bond angles forced by the folded four membered and triangular faces with the ideal angles for sp2 and sp3 carbon.
walkthrough:
See the strain in the cages**
Delocalised benzene can keep perfect $120^{\circ}$ angles. Dewar and Ladenburg force carbons into small folded rings with very sharp angles, far from ideal $\text{sp}^2$ $120^{\circ}$ and $\text{sp}^3$ $109.5^{\circ}$. This angle compression creates large ring strain, making them unstable.
Final answer: High bond strain / ring strain due to bond angles distorted a long way from ideal $109.5^{\circ}$ and $120^{\circ}$.

hints: Count distinct types of H by symmetry: all identical H give 1 peak, alkene H versus alkane bridgehead H are different.
walkthrough:
Count symmetry unique protons**
Delocalised benzene has all 6 H equivalent by sixfold symmetry, so 1 peak. Ladenburg prismane also has all 6 H equivalent, so 1 peak. Dewar has 4 vinylic $\text{sp}^2$ H in one environment and 2 bridgehead $\text{sp}^3$ H in another, so 2 peaks.
Final answer: Dewar benzene: 2 peaks, Ladenburg benzene: 1 peak, delocalised benzene: 1 peak.

hints: Remember how FeBr3 as a Lewis acid pulls off Br- from an alkyl bromide to leave a carbocation, forming FeBr4-.
walkthrough:
Make the carbocation electrophile**
$\text{FeBr}_3$ accepts a bromide ion from one end of 1,4-dibromobutane, just like $\text{AlCl}_3$ in normal alkylation. The $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks heterolytically to give the primary carbocation $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ and the $\text{FeBr}_4^-$ counter ion.
Final answer: $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{FeBr}_3 \rightarrow \text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+ + \text{FeBr}_4^-$

hints: Start with the pi electrons of the phenylethanone ring attacking the carbocation electrophile.
Recall the intermediate is a positively charged arenium ion with the new alkyl group attached and H still present at that carbon.
Think about how aromaticity is restored by breaking the C-H bond at the site of attack.
walkthrough:
Attack of the ring on the electrophile**
Draw a curly arrow from inside the benzene hexagon to the $^+$ carbon of $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$. The pi pair forms the new $\text{C-C}$ bond at the meta position to the deactivating $\text{COCH}_3$ group.

Draw the Wheland intermediate**
The ring now loses aromaticity and carries a positive charge delocalised over the other carbons. Show the cyclohexadienyl cation with the $\text{COCH}_3$ group still attached and the new $\text{-(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{Br}$ group plus H on the tetrahedral carbon.

Restore aromaticity**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond at that tetrahedral carbon back into the ring to reform the pi system, releasing $\text{H}^+$. This gives the meta alkylated product shown plus $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system to $\text{C}^+$ of $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ to give arenium / Wheland intermediate with positive charge delocalised in ring and Br(CH2)4 group attached meta to $\text{COCH}_3$.
Curly arrow from C-H bond back into ring to reform aromatic pi system, expelling $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Use the molecular formulas to decide if the by-product uses one or two phenylethanone units with the C4 chain.
Consider what happens if both Br ends react, either with two separate rings or by the second end looping back onto the same ring.
walkthrough:
Identify Y as double intermolecular alkylation**
$\text{C}_{20}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_2$ is exactly two $\text{C}_8\text{H}_7\text{O}$ phenylethanone fragments plus $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$. That means both Br atoms of $\text{Br(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{Br}$ have alkylated two separate phenylethanone molecules. Draw two meta-acetylphenyl rings joined by $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-$ at the meta positions.

Identify Z as intramolecular ring closure**
$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$ is the normal product $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{15}\text{OBr}$ minus $\text{HBr}$. After the first meta alkylation, the terminal $-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ forms a second carbocation and attacks the same ring intramolecularly. This closes a new 6-membered aliphatic ring fused to the benzene, giving an acetyl-substituted tetralin.

Final answer: Y ($\text{C}_{20}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_2$): $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COCH}_3$ with both alkyl links meta to acetyl, i.e. 1,4-bis(3-acetylphenyl)butane.
Z ($\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$): intramolecular cyclisation to form a fused 6-membered aliphatic ring, i.e. acetyl-tetralin with acetyl ortho or para to the fused ring.
